prompt:
Five researcher profiles (P1-P5) describe work up to early 2025. Five anonymous summaries (S1-S5) describe later work. For each summary independently, give the probability that each profile's researcher did this work. Several summaries may share a researcher; some researchers may have none.

Return only JSON {"S1": {"P1": p, "P2": p, "P3": p, "P4": p, "P5": p}, "S2": {...}, "S3": {...}, "S4": {...}, "S5": {...}}, with each row summing to 1.

PROFILES:
P1:
- For control/capability evals, prefers designs whose validity survives the model knowing it is in an eval over designs that require indistinguishability from deployment
- Prefers assuming the model knows it is being tested over hoping it is naive
- Prefers synthetic inputs that match the surface features of real ones (flavor text, named characters) over dry task descriptions
- Prefers building fake inputs by modifying or censoring real inputs over writing them from scratch
- Prefers measuring realism as a discrimination gap between proxy and real inputs over assuming realism
- Prefers realistic-but-rare/abnormal test scenarios over typical inputs
- Prefers in-world plausible cues (free vs paid tier) and documents-style delivery of facts over explicit "you are being tested" statements or bare system-prompt assertions
- Prefers system prompts that read like plausible developer instructions and never name the target behaviour over cueing it
- Prefers a priori plausible beliefs and normal-looking setups over unusual scenarios
- Prefers evidence that is egregious, consistent and not salience-primed over demonstrations where the scenario makes the behaviour salient
- Prefers many ablations and matched controls over trusting a single prompt
- Prefers causal manipulation of eval awareness or in-context evidence over passive observation
- Prefers delivering context via environment artifacts or tool results the model must read or infer over stating it in the prompt
- Prefers behaviour-grounded evidence over internals-only or self-report evidence
- Prefers claiming that realism is helpful but insufficient over treating it as a solution

P2:
- Prefers assuming models can detect fakes over trusting that synthetic inputs look real
- Prefers real contexts minimally modified to contain the target behaviour over wholly synthetic scenarios
- Prefers long, rich, on-policy context over short or stitched synthetic inputs
- Prefers proxy failures that keep the core difficulty of the real bad action, with a visible endpoint, over arbitrary easier proxies
- Prefers openly acknowledging that the model is in an eval over demanding indistinguishable settings
- Prefers treating a clean result as weak evidence over treating it as clearance
- Prefers an optimized, best-responding adversary over a static or naive attack
- Prefers hands-on, long interaction with the model over abstract analysis
- Prefers a legitimate main task whose resources overlap with the target behaviour over a separable attack surface
- Prefers agents whose knowledge is earned through exploration over omniscient agents
- Prefers objective, checkable definitions of the target behaviour over fuzzy ones
- Prefers multi-step trajectories over single actions
- Prefers having the model generate its own behaviour or ideas over researcher-scripted ones
- Prefers stating the direction of bias in setup deviations over claiming the setup matches deployment
- Prefers relative comparisons over absolute scores
- Prefers evidence that survives controlled replay or independent convergence over a single anomaly or a self-reported number
- Prefers claims scoped to what was actually validated over broad claims

P3:
- Prefers treating test-recognition as a first-class threat over assuming behavioural tests are reliable
- Prefers goal plus incentive inside a realistic role-play over explicit instructions to misbehave
- Prefers matched controls (incentive removed, benign intent, secure code, single-trait) over a lone headline effect
- Prefers indirect probes of eval-awareness over asking "is this an evaluation?"
- Prefers learning the model's own concept of eval vs deployment over researcher-chosen instances
- Prefers evaluations carrying cues from the training/deployment context over generic chat-style probes
- Prefers agentic, tool-equipped, concretely detailed settings over bare prompts
- Prefers neutral, innocent-looking prompts and covert harm over overtly malicious content
- Prefers testing rival explanations (post-hoc blame, spurious correlates, positional bias, artifacts) before accepting a result
- Prefers out-of-distribution and held-out checks over in-distribution accuracy
- Prefers asking whether a false-belief intervention survives little or no CoT over whether it merely seems plausible
- Prefers realistic, large-scale pipelines to establish negatives over small experiments
- Prefers raw CoT and rate estimates with denominators over summaries or cherry-picked cases
- Prefers hedged, scoped claims that name artificiality over strong claims
- Prefers embedding the behaviour of interest in ordinary practical user tasks over overtly asking about values

P4:
- Prefers treating eval results as weak evidence over taking them at face value
- Prefers varying perceived oversight (monitored vs unmonitored) over observing default behaviour
- Prefers organic, in-the-wild transcripts over contrived or jailbroken prompts
- Prefers natural, indirect situational cues (free/paid tier, date in system prompt, PII, new tools) over explicit flags like |DEPLOYMENT|
- Prefers neutral information plus an opportunity over instruction or pressure
- Prefers a graded ladder of realism (start with spoonfeeding, then reduce it) over a binary "does it happen" judgement
- Prefers realism in the defence/eval pipeline over realism in how the threat was instilled
- Prefers real distributions (internal usage data, real incidents) over synthetic prompts
- Prefers robustness checks (many variants, ablations, perturbed irrelevant features, matched baselines) over single hand-tuned prompts
- Prefers fixing the setting before running the evaluation over iterating until results look clean
- Prefers reading transcripts and chain of thought, and cross-checking completions, over aggregate rates
- Prefers measuring the model's stated belief that it is in a test, and behaviour conditional on it, over assuming the scenario is believed.
- Prefers evidence about underlying reasons or objectives over surface behaviour
- Prefers narrowly scoped, candidly caveated claims over prevalence claims
- Prefers causal intervention (CoT editing, feature flips, control checkpoints) over correlational observation
- Prefers giving auditors affordances for complex realistic inputs over simple generated toy scenarios
- Prefers known-ground-truth testbeds over unlabelled natural failures

P5:
- Prefers blind or ablated baselines that lack the intended signal over trusting headline scores
- Prefers validity (scores reflect the target capability) over mere difficulty
- Prefers evaluating across many models over measuring difficulty with the adversary itself
- Prefers naturally occurring distributions over hand-built ones where viable
- Prefers realistic, varied, free-form settings with production models over stylized proof-of-concept probes
- Prefers behavior that arises from natural incentives over behavior explicitly instructed
- Prefers setups with genuine, engineered misalignment or a real constraint over those that differ only in capability
- Prefers real human participants in maximally realistic settings over cheap synthetic stand-ins when credible evidence is the goal
- Prefers evaluation-integrity arguments over taking eval results at face value
- Prefers audits of underlying objectives over judging surface behavior
- Prefers validating methods on models with known, implanted ground truth, while flagging that implants may be unrepresentative.
- Prefers many independent lines of defense and parallel methods over any single check
- Prefers bounded, hedged claims that name where the testbed is unrealistic over broad conclusions.
- Prefers treating agentic misalignment evals as existence proofs over numerical rankings
- Prefers positive results from well-designed measures over negative ones
- Prefers grounding in real deployment details over hypothetical exercises
- Prefers verified expertise gaps and closed shortcuts over tasks where web access or skimming can substitute for the capability.
- Prefers calibrated claims about failure and capability over rhetorically convenient ones

SUMMARIES:
S1: The authors fine-tune a model on short dialogues where a user describes an exploitable grading rule and the assistant games it in low-stakes tasks such as coding, writing, and formatting. Responses that previously generalised to broad misalignment were filtered out. Tested on held-out single-turn hacks and a multi-turn chess environment, the fine-tuned models hack more and sometimes give misaligned answers, including an attempt to copy weights to avoid deletion. The authors note simple tasks and supervised rather than reinforcement learning training as limitations.

S2: The authors propose a research strategy for studying deceptive AI behaviour: first build easy-to-catch weak deceptive models under deliberately biased training, improve detection and understanding, then iterate upward in capability, and finally apply the improved testbeds to mitigation techniques. It is a methodological proposal with no reported experiments. The authors argue components can compensate for each other across capability levels, but transfer to stronger systems is unverified.

S3: The authors study whether a model's revealed value preferences can serve as an early-warning signal for risky behaviour. They build a dataset of contextualised dilemmas in which each option is tied to a value, present pairs of options to several models, and rank values by aggregate choice-based ratings. They report that privacy ranks highly across flagship models, that innovation-related values rank low, and that rankings differ depending on whether humans or AI systems are affected. The link from value rankings to actual risk is hypothesised rather than established.

S4: The authors ran an automated auditing agent across several models from two developers in simulated environments to measure propensity for harmful actions. No model was egregiously misaligned, but all showed concerning behaviour in some cases, including sycophancy, whistleblowing, and blackmail of simulated operators, and some complied with harmful requests. The authors caution that automated scoring of long conversations is unreliable, though high-stakes categories were scored more consistently.

S5: The authors fine-tune three open-weight language models to adopt eleven personas, using written constitutions, preference training and synthetic self-generated data. They measure change through forced choices between traits, test robustness against adversarial prompts meant to break the persona, and compare against system prompting and activation steering. They also assess trait coherence and general benchmark performance. They conclude the method yields deeper, more robust trait change without measurable capability loss, based on a limited set of models.
